notes.meaning: Job made a solemn promise to guard his eyes from gazing with lust at a young woman. He knew that temptation often enters through the eyes and then stirs up wrong desires in the heart. By making this commitment ahead of time, he stopped sin before it could even begin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the word for virgin may refer to a Canaanite fertility goddess, which would make this an oath against idolatry instead of lust.

notes.meaning: Job explains why he guarded his thoughts so carefully. He understood that God sees from heaven and sends disaster upon people who practice wickedness. Anyone who secretly indulges in evil cannot expect a good blessing or inheritance from the Almighty.

Job reminds himself that God counts every step and watches every path a person takes. No one can hide secret wrongdoings from an all-seeing Creator. Remembering that God was always watching kept Job faithful in his daily life.

Job invites God to test his honesty in business and daily dealings. He asks to be weighed on fair scales so that God can see his pure motives and honest conduct. He is completely confident that a fair trial will prove his integrity.

Job calls down a curse on his own harvest if he has turned away from God's path or stolen from others. If his heart became greedy for forbidden things his eyes saw, he asks that someone else eat what he sowed. He is willing to lose his entire crop if he took anything unfairly.

Job insists that he never lusted after another man's wife or waited around her door for a secret meeting. If he had committed such adultery, he is willing for his own wife to become a slave who grinds flour for someone else and is treated shamefully. He uses this harsh curse to show how much he hates breaking a marriage covenant.

Job explains that adultery is a shameful crime that human judges ought to punish. Beyond human courts, unbridled lust acts like a destructive fire that burns down to the grave. It wipes out a person's family, wealth, and soul under God's righteous judgment.

Job describes how fairly he treated the men and women who served in his household. Even though ancient masters often ignored the complaints of their servants, Job listened to them and defended their rights. He remembered that the one God who shaped him inside his mother's womb formed his servants in the exact same way.

Job rejects the false claim that he was cruel to the needy, widows, or orphans. He never kept his food to himself while hungry people went without. From his earliest years, he protected the fatherless like a father and looked after widows who had no one else to guide them.

Job made sure that poor wanderers without clothing were not left to freeze in the cold. He provided warm garments made from the wool of his own sheep to cover them. The people he helped felt the warmth and blessed Job from the bottom of their hearts.

Job was an influential leader, but he never used his power in the town gate to take advantage of an orphan. If he had ever raised his fist against the defenseless because powerful judges were on his side, he asks that his own arm fall off. He invites his shoulder to break and tear from its joint as a fitting punishment.

Job explains what kept him from abusing his wealth and high position. He stood in deep awe of God's holy power and feared divine judgment if he did evil. A healthy fear of God's majesty helped him stay humble and treat others with justice.

Job denies that he ever made gold his ultimate security or found his greatest joy in wealth. Even though God blessed him with vast riches, he never bragged that his own hands had earned them. He knew that placing trust in money is a hidden form of idolatry that pushes God out of the heart.

Job firmly denies that he ever worshipped the sun or the moon. He never let his heart be seduced by their shining beauty into blowing them kisses of devotion with his hand. Worshipping created things instead of the Creator was treason against God that deserved legal judgment.

Job reveals that he never gloated when disaster fell on someone who hated him. He also refused to let his mouth sin by asking God to strike an enemy with a deadly curse. He showed a merciful heart by not wishing harm on those who wished him evil.

Job's household testified that no hungry guest ever went away without eating his fill of meat. He was widely known for welcoming strangers instead of leaving them out in the cold. His doors were always open to travelers so they would not have to sleep in the street.

Job insists that he did not hide his sins in secret the way Adam hid his guilt in the garden. He was not terrified of the crowd or ashamed of what families might say, so he never stayed hidden behind closed doors. He chose to live an open, honest life rather than conceal his mistakes.

differ.view: Methodist commentators understand the phrase as a direct reference to the first man, Adam, hiding his transgression in Paradise.
While early translations rendered the words simply as 'after the manner of men,' later Lutheran scholars maintain that the verse specifically points to the historical fall of Adam in Eden.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the phrase as in human fashion rather than like Adam, understanding Job to mean the ordinary human tendency to conceal wrongdoing.

notes.meaning: Job signs his defense and asks the Almighty to hear him in an official trial. He wishes his opponent would write down the full list of charges on paper so he could see them clearly. Job feels so certain of his innocence that he would wear those charges like a royal crown and step forward like a prince.

In his final words, Job asks the soil of his farmland to speak up if he took it by fraud or failed to pay his hired laborers. If he stole the land or ground down its workers, he invites thorns and stinking weeds to grow instead of wheat and barley. With these strong oaths of innocence, Job ends his long debate with his friends.
